paper.title: Learning to Bid Without Knowing your Value

unmapped: Win-only feedback: adversary picks reward function r_t: B->[-1,1] and allocation function x_t: B->[0,1]; reward won w.p. x_t(b); learner always observes the whole allocation function x_t(.) and observes the whole reward function r_t(.) only if the reward is won
Application: repeated auctions with unknown value (bidder observes value only when winning)
settings.definition_quote: Every day a learner picks an action $b_t$ from a finite set $B$. The adversary chooses a reward function $r_t: B\rightarrow [-1,1]$ and an allocation function $x_t: B \rightarrow [0,1]$. The learner wins a reward $r_t(b)$ with probability $x_t(b)$. ... After each iteration, if she won the reward then she learns the whole reward function $r_t(\cdot)$, while she \emph{always} learns the allocation function $x_t(\cdot)$.

unmapped: Outcome-based feedback: finite outcome set O (size n_out); adversary picks reward r_t: B x O -> [-1,1] and allocation x_t: B -> Delta(O); outcome o_t ~ x_t(b_t); learner observes r_t(., o_t) for all actions and always the full allocation function x_t(.)
Learner knows the number of outcomes |O| (used in step size)
settings.definition_quote: Every day a learner picks an action $b_t$ from a finite set $B$. There is a set of payoff-relevant outcomes $O$. The adversary chooses a reward function $r_t: B\times O\rightarrow [-1,1]$ ... and he also chooses an allocation function $x_t: B \rightarrow \Delta(O)$ ... The learner wins reward $r_t(b_t, o_t)$ and observes the whole outcome-specific reward function $r_t(\cdot, o_t)$. She \emph{always} learns the allocation function $x_t(\cdot)$ after the iteration.

unmapped: Each iteration has a set of reward contests I_t; same action used in all; outcomes drawn independently from x_t(b_t) per contest; utility is the average reward; learner observes average outcome-conditional reward functions Q_t(b,o), realized outcome frequencies f_t(o), and the allocation function x_t
Learner knows the number of outcomes |O|
settings.definition_quote: Every iteration $t$ is associated with a set of \emph{reward contests} $I_t$. The learner picks an action $b_t$, which is used at \emph{all} reward contests. For each $\tau\in I_t$ the adversary picks an outcome specific reward function $r_\tau: B\times O \rightarrow [-1,1]$. Moreover, the adversary chooses an allocation function $x_t: B\rightarrow \Delta(O)$, which is not $\tau$-dependent.

settings.name_in_paper: Continuous actions with Delta^o-Piecewise Lipschitz average utilities (outcome-based feedback with batch rewards)
unmapped: Action space [0,1]^d; average utility is Delta^o-piecewise L-Lipschitz (cubes of edge >= Delta^o, L-Lipschitz in l_inf within each cube, boundary points dominated by limits of interior points)
Outcome-based batch-reward feedback as in the batch setting
settings.definition_quote: A learning setting with action space $\B=[0,1]^d$, is said to have $\Delta^o$-Piecewise Lipschitz Cumulative Utilities if the average utility function $\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^T u_t(b)$ satisfies the following conditions: the bidding space $[0,1]^d$ is divided into $d$-dimensional cubes with edge length at least $\Delta^o$ and within each cube the utility is $L$-Lipschitz with respect to the $\ell_{\infty}$ norm.

settings.name_in_paper: Continuous actions with piecewise Lipschitz utilities, unknown L, T, Delta^o (doubling trick)
unmapped: Action space [0,1]^d with Delta^o-piecewise L-Lipschitz average utilities; L, T and Delta^o unknown (handled by doubling)
settings.definition_quote: In order to address the problem that in general we do not know any of those constants a priori, we will apply a standard doubling trick ... We assume that $T$ is upper bounded by a constant $T_M$ and similarly we also assume that $\log\left(\max\left\{LT, \frac{1}{\Delta^o}\right\}\right)$ is upper bounded by a constant.

settings.name_in_paper: Sponsored search (weighted GSP) with continuous bids and Lipschitz utilities
unmapped: Value-per-click sponsored search with weighted GSP; quality scores drawn i.i.d. from L-Lipschitz CDFs; reserve lower bounded by delta; bids in [0,1]; learner observes CTR and CPC curves and average click value when clicked (batch rewards, |O|=2)
The learner knows the number of bidders n, the CDF Lipschitz constant L and the reserve lower bound delta (used in the grid size)
settings.definition_quote: when the quality scores in sponsored search are drawn from $L$-Lipschitz CDFs $F_i, \forall i \in n$ and the reserve is lower bounded by $\delta>0$, then the utilities are $\frac{2nL}{\delta}$-Lipschitz

settings.name_in_paper: Switching regret with outcome-based feedback (continuous piecewise Lipschitz actions)
unmapped: Regret against a sequence of bids with at most C switches
Action space [0,1]^d with Delta^o-piecewise L-Lipschitz utilities; outcome-based feedback
settings.definition_quote: Let $C \geq 0$ be the number of times that the optimal bid $b^* \in \B$ switches in a horizon of $T$ rounds.

settings.name_in_paper: Outcome-based feedback with a feedback graph over outcomes
unmapped: Directed feedback graph G over OUTCOMES (not actions), with self-loops; when outcome o_t realizes the learner observes r_t(., o) for all o in the out-neighbourhood of o_t; alpha_G is the independence number of this outcome graph
Learner knows |O| and the outcome graph
settings.definition_quote: We now extend Section \ref{sec:continuous}, by assuming that there is a directed feedback graph $G=(O, E)$ over the outcomes. When outcome $o_t$ is chosen, the bidder observes not only the outcome specific reward function $r_t(\cdot, o_t)$, for that outcome, but also for any outcome $o$ in the out-neighborhood of $o_t$ in the feedback graph

algorithms.name: Randomized Tracking Algorithm (Algorithm 2 of Gyorgy et al. 2012) with A = WIN-EXP

source.label: thm:win-only-regr
source.quote: The regret of the $\winexp$ algorithm with the aforementioned unbiased estimates and step size $\sqrt{\frac{2\log(|B|)}{5T}}$ is: $4\sqrt{T\log(|B|)}$.

results.notes: Regret defined as sup_b E[sum u_t(b*) - u_t(b_t)] with expected (over outcome) utilities, hence pseudo_regret. Proof gives 2*sqrt(10/2)... sqrt(10 T log|B|) <= 4 sqrt(T log|B|). Feedback mapped to partial_monitoring (win-only).

source.label: thm:outcome-based-main
source.quote: The regret of Algorithm \ref{alg:winexp2} with $\tilde{u}_t(b) = \frac{(r_t(b, o_t) - 1) \Pr_t[o_t | b]}{\Pr_t[o_t]}$ and step size $\sqrt{\frac{\log(|B|)}{2T|O|}}$ is: $2\sqrt{2T|O|\log(|B|)}$.

results.notes: Examples 4.2-4.4 instantiate this (|O|=2 gives 4 sqrt(T log|B|); unit-demand K items gives 2 sqrt(2(K+1)T log|B|)).

source.label: corol:batch-rewards
source.quote: The $\winexp$ algorithm with the latter unbiased utility estimates and step size $\sqrt{\frac{\log(|B|)}{2T|O|}}$, achieves regret in the outcome-based feedback with batch rewards setting at most: $2\sqrt{2T|O|\log(|B|)}$.

results.notes: Regret on average-per-contest utilities. Sponsored search example (|O|=2) gives 4 sqrt(T log|B|).

symbols.Delta_o: minimum edge length of the cubes on which the average utility is Lipschitz

conditions: average utility is Delta^o-piecewise L-Lipschitz (l_inf) on [0,1]^d
tuning: uniform eps-grid with eps = min{1/(LT), Delta^o}

source.label: thm:continuous-lipschitz-known
source.quote: Let $\B=[0,1]^d$ be the action space as defined in our model and let $B$ be a uniform $\eps$-grid of $\B$. The $\winexp$ algorithm ... on $B$ with $\eta = \sqrt{\frac{\log(|B|)}{2T|O|}}$, $\eps=\min \left\{\frac{1}{L T},\Delta^o \right\}$ achieves expected regret at most $2\sqrt{2T|O|d\log \left(\max\left\{\frac{1}{\Delta^o},LT\right\} \right)} + 1$ in the outcome-based feedback with batch rewards and $\Delta^o$-Piecewise $L-$Lipschitz average utilities

results.notes: Regret against best fixed bid in continuous [0,1]^d. Example 5.5 (first-price/all-pay, d=1,|O|=2,L=1) gives 4 sqrt(T log max{1/Delta^o,T})+1.

symbols.Delta_o: minimum edge length of the Lipschitz cubes

conditions: average utility is Delta^o-piecewise L-Lipschitz on [0,1]^d
T is upper bounded by a constant T_M and log(max{LT,1/Delta^o}) is upper bounded by a constant

source.label: cor:doubling
source.quote: The $\winexp$ algorithm run with the above doubling trick achieves an expected regret bound $\mathcal{R}(T) \leq 25\sqrt{2dT|O|\log\left(\max \left\{LT, \frac{1}{\Delta^o} \right\}\right)} +1$

results.notes: Proof is loose (e.g. log terms absorbed); recorded as stated. Horizon treated as unknown via doubling.

symbols.L_cdf: Lipschitz constant of the quality-score CDFs
symbols.delta_r: lower bound on the reserve price (not a failure probability)

conditions: weighted GSP with quality scores drawn independently from L-Lipschitz CDFs

source.quote: The $\winexp$ algorithm run on a uniform $\epsilon$-grid with $\epsilon = \frac{\delta}{2nLT}$, step size $\sqrt{\frac{\log(1/\epsilon)}{4T}}$ and unbiased estimates ... when applied to the sponsored search auction setting with quality scores drawn independently from distributions with $L$-Lipschitz CDFs, achieves regret at most: $4\sqrt{T\log\left(\frac{2nLT}{\delta}\right)}+1$.

results.notes: Utilities are 2nL/delta-Lipschitz by Theorem 5.7 (structural, not a regret result).

symbols.Delta_o: minimum edge length of the Lipschitz cubes
symbols.alpha_g: algorithm parameter alpha in (0,1) of the tracking algorithm (g+1 = (T/(C+1))^alpha)

conditions: optimal bid switches at most C times (paper's C = S_T)

source.label: cor:switch
source.quote: Let $C \geq 0$ be the number of times that the optimal bid $b^* \in \B$ switches in a horizon of $T$ rounds. Then, using Algorithm $2$ in \cite{GLL12} with $\mathcal{A} \equiv \winexp$ and any $\alpha \in (0,1)$ we can achieve expected \emph{switching regret} at most: $O \left( \sqrt{\left(C+1 \right)^2 \left( 2 + \frac{1}{\alpha} \right) 2d |O| T \log \left(\max \left\{ LT, \frac{1}{\Delta^o} \right\} \right)}\right)$

results.notes: Paper's C (number of switches) mapped to S_T. Whether learner needs to know C is unclear.

symbols.alpha_G: independence number of the feedback graph over outcomes

conditions: feedback graph over outcomes includes self-loops
tuning: eta = sqrt(log|B| / (8 T alpha ln(16|O|^2 T/alpha)))

source.label: thm:feedback-graph
source.quote: The regret of the $\winexpG$ algorithm with step size $\eta = \sqrt{\frac{\log(|B|)}{8T\alpha \ln\left(\frac{16|O|^2 T}{\alpha}\right)}}$ is bounded by: $R(T) \leq 2 \sqrt{8\alpha T \log(|B|) \ln\left(\frac{16|O|^2 T}{\alpha}\right)} + 1$.

results.notes: alpha_G here is the independence number of a graph over outcomes, not actions.
